candidates.title: Trusted Computing Group Creates Key New Working Group Focusing on Aerospace Security
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Trusted Computing Group (TCG) has created a new Aerospace and Non-Terrestrial Systems Solutions Working Group (AERO-SWG) as it looks to play a key role in keeping satellite systems secure. Focusing on satellite networks, unmanned systems, autonomous platforms, and disconnected edge environments, AERO-SWG will aim to help operators apply trusted computing principles to strengthen the resilience and integrity of the systems now central to global communications and critical infrastructure. TCG announced the new group, Sept. 29. AERO-SWG will aim to establish trust within the devices, platforms, gateways, and supply chains that underpin the global communications, defense, transportation, and critical infrastructure society now relies upon. This will be achieved through practical guidance, gap analysis, and recommendations to existing TCG Work Groups. The group will be chaired by TCG member Thorsten Stremlau of Nvidia. AERO-SWG will explore how layered hardware and firmware security can be applied across aircraft, satellites and ground stations to strengthen trust at the platform level. This includes Trusted Platform Modile (TPM)-based Roots-of-Trust for flight-critical software, Device Identifier Composition Engine (DICE) for lightweight subsystem protection, and CyRes for restoring corrupted firmware in flight or in orbit. “AERO-SWG gives the industry a dedicated forum to ensure trusted computing in the toughest aerospace environments, including satellites and autonomous systems. By bringing experts together to focus on practical needs and real deployment barriers, the group will help accelerate the development of secure and interoperable technologies in this crucial sector,” Joe Pennisi, president of TCG, said in a statement. candidates.raw_excerpt: The FCC continued its push to deregulate and open up new spectrum with two major decisions on Wednesday — exempting space activities from certain federal environmental regulations and opening up 1,000 megahertz of spectrum. W-8 will carry sensors to study the capsule’s temperature and other data during re-entry, and includes thermal protection materials on the outside under a US military study. Their study, published in the research journal Joule , outlines a new type of solar panel built with perovskites — a calcium titanium oxide mineral — instead of silicon. By using pervoskite-based cells, the researchers were able to adjust the solar panels to capitalize on the kinds of blue and green sunlight waves that can penetrate the ocean’s surface. According to the paper, the peak power conversion efficiency — a measure of how much sunlight hitting a panel is converted into usable energy — reached a high of nearly 35 percent. If true, that figure puts the panels in-line with recent breakthrough research in solar cell efficiency, and a notch above the long-established Shockley-Queisser limit , a theoretical cap which limited photovoltaic efficiency to about 33 percent. Granted, the results were obtained under simulation conditions, so more rigorous testing is needed to confirm whether similar results are possible in a real-world setting. Overall, the test ran for just two hours, generating 324 milliwatt-hours, enough to power a small LED light for a few hours. Still, even sniffing the Shockley-Queisser limit with solar panels some 30 feet underwater is a noteworthy accomplishment. And as EuroNews observes, even the decidedly small amount of electricity produced far surpassed researchers’ expectations. candidates.title: CNES Publishes Call for New Rocket Launch Tracking Turrets for French Guiana
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: CSG The French space agency CNES has issued a call for new automated optical tracking systems for the Guiana Space Centre. The new system will need to be capable of tracking launch vehicles to altitudes of up to an altitude of 100 kilometres. Published on 24 September , the initiative aims to replace aging and partially obsolete equipment currently used to capture imagery of Ariane and Vega launches. CNES said the existing systems are ageing and partially obsolete. The agency wants to replace the manual and semi-automated systems with a fully automated alternative, with tracking tied directly to launch vehicle trajectory data. Beyond launch imagery for public broadcasts, the spaceport’s flight-safety teams use these systems for technical analysis and diagnostics to support post-launch investigations. The new tracking turrets will carry sensors operating in both the visible and infrared spectrum, together with very-long-focal-length optics capable of clearly observing a launch vehicle at an altitude of 100 kilometres. In total, CNES plans to procure three turrets. Two will be fixed systems, while the third will be a mobile unit that can be positioned where it’s needed. CNES will install one fixed turret on Île Royale, an island off the coast of French Guiana, and the second on the mainland. The turrets will be managed remotely and operated from a single console at the Image Production Centre (Centre de Production d’Images) in the Jupiter 2 building, which is also home to the spaceport’s main control centre. CNES expects to award the contract in the third quarter of 2027. The contract, covering the supply, installation and qualification of the new systems, is expected to run for approximately three years.
